哈撥琴出現在搖滾樂團、流行現場、影視原聲帶與電視表演中。Jordan Rudes: The harpejji appears in rock bands, live pop shows, film and television soundtracks and television performances. Jordan Rudess has used it with Dream Theater and recorded it for the soundtrack of the video game God of War III; Stevie Wonder played “Superstition” on it at the Billboard Music Awards and has shared a stage with the Dave Matthews Band. A. R. Rahman used it for the song “If I Rise” in the film 127 Hours and on India's Coke Studio; there is also a music video, a television programme and album tracks in which four people play at once.
哈撥琴是美國音訊工程師 Tim Meeks 於2007年開發的電子弦鳴樂器，有1: The harpejji is an electronic chordophone developed in 2007 by the American audio engineer Tim Meeks. It has 12 to 24 strings, stands on a support like a keyboard, and the strings run perpendicular to the player. The playing surface is laid out in whole tones across and semitones lengthwise, and it is played mainly by tapping with both hands, all ten fingers being able to press strings. Jordan Rudess, Stevie Wonder, A. R. Rahman and others have used it in recordings, live performance and television programmes.
哈撥琴為電子弦鳴樂器，以弦振動發聲。演奏以雙手點弦為主，電子靜音系統抑制未按弦，: The harpejji is an electronic chordophone and sounds by the vibration of its strings. It is played mainly by tapping with both hands, and an electronic muting system suppresses strings that are not being pressed, reducing unwanted resonance. The 24-string model has a range from A0 to A5 and the 22-string M5 from C1 to C6, both five octaves. Unlike tapping instruments such as the Chapman Stick, it stands on a support with its surface like a keyboard and the strings perpendicular to the player, so all ten fingers can press strings and one hand can cover two octaves; it can also be strummed with a pick. The source does not mention how volume is controlled.

The source states clearly only that later 24-string models changed the main wood from maple to bamboo; as for the other parts of the body, the string material, the electronics and the material of the support, the source does not say.
哈撥琴由美國音訊工程師Tim Meeks於2007年開發，名稱取自harp與ar: The harpejji was developed in 2007 by the American audio engineer Tim Meeks, taking its name from harp and arpeggio, and can be traced back to the StarrBoard developed in the 1980s. The first model, the D1, was made from January 2008 to May 2010 and was then replaced by the K24, with updated internal electronics, simplified surface markings and the main wood changed from maple to bamboo. The 16-string G16 followed in January 2011, and later the Msf, M5 and U12. About 500 had been made by 2019, and through recordings and performances by Jordan Rudess, Stevie Wonder, A. R. Rahman and others it entered pop, film and television settings.
持琴時，哈撥琴置於支架上，琴面如鍵盤，弦垂直於演奏者。發聲主要採雙手點弦，以十指: To hold it, the harpejji stands on its support with its surface like a keyboard and the strings perpendicular to the player. It sounds mainly by tapping with both hands, pressing the strings with all ten fingers, while an electronic muting system suppresses the resonance of strings not being pressed. A beginner can first get used to the layout, whole tones along the strings and semitones across, and practise fingerings that span two octaves with one hand; strumming with a pick can also be tried. There is no official method book yet.
